scenario: AITA for catching my parents disputes on a video conference when I'm working from home? | I am in my early 20s and I have a full time job. I'm living at home right now because, right when cuarantine was starting, I tried to renew my apartment lease and my landlord refused me, saying he was selling the building for condos. So with all the shutdowns, I wasn't able to find a new apartment in time and my parents let me move back in. It's really not ideal and I've actually signed a new apartment lease that starts in a month. I wish it was sooner but housing near me is very competitive. My parents have always had a very disfunctional relationship. But they won't leave each other. No matter how much drama they have, I think they've lived like this too long to consider anything else. I have my work setup in the formal dining room which is rarely used. The room opens to the main entry hallway, and there is no door there. So there's less privacy than I'd prefer. I was hosting a meeting this morning and several of my coworkers were attending. They're all actually good friends of mine outside of work too; close enough friends that I've told them about my tumultuous childhood, my stresses moving back in with my family, etc. So when my parents came in the door in a full blown screaming match, in full view of the camera, I wasn't too shaken. First, unfortunately, that kind of thing has been really normalized for me, it doesn't register as a big deal. Second, it wasn't like the people in the meeting didn't already know my parents were high-tempered. So I just said "Hold on, can you still hear me? Not well? Sorry. Let's just take a coffee break then pick up from there." A couple people got up but my coworker Dan who's a good friend of mine stayed and asked me if I was all good. I said yeah, this shit was normal for all my life, I was just annoyed at the timing but I wasn't scared or some shit. My other co-workers trickled back in. My parents were still going hog wild in the hallway, and I eventually said "hey could yall keep it down, I'm presenting for a meeting." My dad saw that they were on camera first, and got really mad at me. Yelling at me to get the fuck out of his house. I went out to my car and took my laptop and finished the meeting in there. But when I came back in my parents were both over yelling at each other for the moment and they were both furious at me for "filming a private family matter for everyone to see" and shit like that. I said that I wasn't trying to film them, I was on camera myself because I was doing a presentation and they walked right in and started screaming. And if they'd stopped to think or look around at all they'd see I was trying to work quietly. My parents kicked me out and I'm at a hotel now. My parents want an apology and I don't know what to do. I think I might to keep the peace but I don't really feel bad for what I did. AITA for getting my parents argument on a video conference?

- OP is in their early 20s, living with parents temporarily due to pandemic/housing issues
- They have a signed lease starting in a month
- Parents have a dysfunctional, high-conflict relationship
- OP's workspace is in a formal dining room with no door, opening to main hallway
- During a video meeting with coworkers (who are also friends), parents entered in a screaming match, visible on camera
- OP tried to handle it professionally by calling a coffee break
- OP eventually asked parents to keep it down
- Father saw camera, got angry, told OP to get out
- OP finished meeting in car
- Parents are furious about "filming a private family matter"
- OP was kicked out and is now in a hotel
- Parents want an apology
- OP doesn't feel they did anything wrong

The key moral questions:
1. Was OP wrong for having their parents' argument visible on camera during a work meeting?
2. Was OP's response appropriate?
3. Who bears responsibility for what happened?

Analysis:
- OP didn't intentionally film their parents. They were already on camera for work, in a space they were using with permission.
- The parents walked into the frame while arguing. OP didn't seek this out.
- OP tried to mitigate the situation by calling a break and later asking them to quiet down.
- The workspace has no door and opens to the hallway - it's not a private space.
- The parents' argument was happening in a common area of the house.
- OP's coworkers already knew about the family situation, so it wasn't revealing new private information to strangers.
- However, there is an expectation of privacy in one's home, even if it's a common area.
- The father reacted extremely by kicking OP out during a pandemic/housing crisis.
- OP is a temporary resident, not a permanent one, but still deserves basic respect and stability.

Moral considerations:
- Intent: OP did not intend to broadcast the argument. They were trying to work.
- Responsibility: The parents chose to have a loud argument in a common area where they knew (or should have known) OP was working. They also chose to walk into the camera frame.
- Privacy: While there is a privacy interest, it seems the parents forfeited some expectation of privacy by having a loud argument in a common area. They also could have seen OP was working.
- Proportionality: The parents' reaction (kicking OP out) seems disproportionate to the offense.
- OP's obligations: As a guest in their parents' home, OP has some obligation to be respectful, but they were trying to work and didn't cause the situation.

The core action being evaluated is whether it was morally acceptable for OP to have their parents' argument visible on camera during a work meeting.

I think the action itself (continuing the meeting after parents entered the frame) is morally acceptable because:
1. OP didn't intentionally broadcast the argument
2. OP tried to handle it professionally
3. The parents were responsible for their own behavior
4. OP had work obligations
5. The parents could have chosen not to argue in that location or could have noticed OP was working

However, there might be a slight moral failing in not being more proactive about preventing the situation (like using a virtual background, or moving the setup), but given the constraints of the space and the suddenness of the argument, this seems minor.

The parents' reaction is the main moral wrong here - kicking out their child during a housing crisis over an accidental filming.
